Review 
Industrial Agentic AI and generative modeling in complex 
systems 
Mohammad Reza Boskabadi1, Yudong Cao2,3,  
Behnam Khadem4, William Clements5, Z. Nevin Gerek6,  
Eric Reuthe2,7, Abhishek Sivaram1, Christopher J Savoie2,7 and  
Seyed Soheil Mansouri1   
Manufacturing, consumer, transportation, and supply chain 
processes present significant challenges in monitoring, control, 
and design due to their inherently nonlinear nature and the 
difficulty of measuring critical variables in real time. The 
convergence of major innovations from the computer science 
field has the potential to revolutionize the engineering and 
control of complex industrial systems. Digital twinning and 
process simulation have been a staple of computers in process 
engineering for decades now. However, the advent of advanced 
sensor systems and big data integration, combined with 
generative AI and agentified AI (classic and quantum) systems, 
allows for much more granular and autonomous process 
control and real-time optimization of complex systems. 
Advanced process modeling, Agentic AI, and generative AI 
models have emerged as powerful tools to address the 
challenges of complex nonlinear systems. We propose here an 
integrated systems feedback and control architecture (SIC: 
Sense, Infer, Control) that leverages complementary process 
knowledge for enhanced real-time monitoring and decision- 
making, fully integrated into control system functions and the 
accompanying sensors. In this paper, we explore this 
integration of generative models in agentic AI ensembles into 
industrial processes through the lens of four recent industrial 
case studies: (1) the real-time optimization of motorsports 
strategy, (2) the development of indirect (soft) sensors for 
sustainable large-scale manufacturing operations, (3) the 
creation of sensor data-driven personalized health and 
cosmetic chemical formulations, and (4) the design of 
biomanufacturing systems using quantum and classic Agentic 
AI. These examples demonstrate how agentic and generative 
models, combined with full-scale process simulation and digital 
twinning, effectively augment process control, enabling 
advanced solutions for process optimization, quality 
improvement, and sustainable operations. The proposed SIC 
systems architecture serves to enhance process control 
automation by capturing complex nonlinear patterns and 
leveraging easily measurable variables. Generative models 
bridge gaps in process understanding, sensor technologies, 
control, and monitoring, offering actionable insights for efficient 
and informed decision-making across diverse industrial 
applications.

sections.heading: Seyed Soheil Mansouri
sections.text: 1 Manufacturing, consumer, transportation, and supply chain processes present significant challenges in monitoring, control, and design due to their inherently nonlinear nature and the difficulty of measuring critical variables in real time. The convergence of major innovations from the computer science field has the potential to revolutionize the engineering and control of complex industrial systems. Digital twinning and process simulation have been a staple of computers in process engineering for decades now. However, the advent of advanced sensor systems and big data integration, combined with generative AI and agentified AI (classic and quantum) systems, allows for much more granular and autonomous process control and real-time optimization of complex systems. Advanced process modeling, Agentic AI, and generative AI models have emerged as powerful tools to address the challenges of complex nonlinear systems. We propose here an integrated systems feedback and control architecture (SIC: Sense, Infer, Control) that leverages complementary process knowledge for enhanced real-time monitoring and decision- making, fully integrated into control system functions and the accompanying sensors. In this paper, we explore this integration of generative models in agentic AI ensembles into industrial processes through the lens of four recent industrial case studies: (1) the real-time optimization of motorsports strategy, (2) the development of indirect (soft) sensors for sustainable large-scale manufacturing operations, (3) the creation of sensor data-driven personalized health and cosmetic chemical formulations, and (4) the design of biomanufacturing systems using quantum and classic Agentic AI. These examples demonstrate how agentic and generative models, combined with full-scale process simulation and digital twinning, effectively augment process control, enabling advanced solutions for process optimization, quality improvement, and sustainable operations. The proposed SIC systems architecture serves to enhance process control automation by capturing complex nonlinear patterns and leveraging easily measurable variables. Generative models bridge gaps in process understanding, sensor technologies, control, and monitoring, offering actionable insights for efficient and informed decision-making across diverse industrial applications. sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: In industrial processes, the primary goals of ensuring safety, enhancing efficiency, reducing costs, and main- taining high-quality standards all motivate the pursuit of improved operations [1–4] . Traditional process control and optimization rely heavily on direct measurements and deterministic models [4] . However, complex sys- tems often involve latent variables that are challenging to measure directly. This limitation necessitates the use of ‘ soft sensors ’ [5] that estimate unobservable variables from measured process data and statistical models, in- cluding agentified and generative models that can infer missing information and optimize control strategies. These soft sensors are surrogates that can be used to estimate the quality indicator variables (QIVs) of process systems, as will be discussed in the individual case stu- dies. These soft sensors and inference models can be implanted in ensembles of semiautonomous granular ]] ]] ]]]]]] www.sciencedirect.com Current Opinion in Chemical Engineering 2025, 48 :101150 inference agents responsible for different areas of in- ference and control decision-making. Ensembles of multiagent inference control architectures have been used since 1990s, and distributed systems of AI agents have been used for complex systems control applications since Adaptive Agent-Oriented Software Architectures (AOSA) was first demonstrated [6] , forming the basis for developing the original versions of Apple’s Siri invented by Hodjat, Savoie, and Amamiya [7••] . This archi- tectural approach enables the generation of real-time estimates essential for process monitoring, providing actionable insights and real-time data for effective pro- cess management and ultimately for control actuation. These modeling architectures utilize multiple sources of both real-time and historical data to identify and re- present complex, nonlinear relationships between critical variables and more easily measurable or detectable proxy variables that are strongly correlated with them [8] . By doing so, such inferences enable the generation of real- time estimates that are a proxy for a direct measurement where direct measurements are not always possible, which is essential for process monitoring and tuning [9•] . Generative models are a class of machine learning algo- rithms designed to generate information and replicate complex data distributions [10,11] . The rapid advancement of generative AI has reshaped various technological sectors [12,13] , yet much of the focus has been on large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT (OpenAI), Gemini (Google), and CoPilot (Microsoft). However, the true po- tential of generative AI extends far beyond text generation. By capturing intricate nonlinear relationships and lever- aging readily available sensor data, statistically driven generative models can fill critical gaps in process under- standing, offering predictive insights and enhanced real- time optimization capabilities. Their integration into in- dustrial workflows enhances decision-making in areas such as predictive maintenance, process optimization, and quality control [14,15] . It is, hence, imperative that suffi- cient process knowledge, in the form of causal connections or dynamical system functionals, be integrated to enable a better understanding of the process [16] . Recent efforts have heavily focused on the use of gen- erative adversarial networks (GANs) aided by recurrent neural networks, long- and short-term memory, and several other models such as diffusive models and similar ap- proaches. However, it is important to note that data dis- tributions can also be driven by mechanistic models, capturing the system’s mean behavior and variance based on underlying measurements [17•] . Despite this potential, challenges remain in ensuring the explainability, inter- pretability, and robustness of generative models in in- dustrial settings. sections.heading: AI and generative modeling
sections.text: We present a systematic approach addressing complex system challenges in process monitoring and control, as illustrated in Figure 1 . This approach consists of three key stages: (1) creating a process and instrumentation workflow to identify critical QIVs for measurement and monitoring, (2) implementing agentified modeling — combining mechanistic modeling and artificial in- telligence — to monitor these QIVs through direct measurement or predictive modeling, and (3) integrating this data into the control system, granting it agency to make real-time decisions for process control. This systematic approach begins with a comprehensive process and instrumentation workflow that defines the process task and maps out all relevant variables — in- cluding process characteristics, dynamic states, process conditions, and critical QIVs — into a structured knowledge base. This base comprises mechanistic models, parametric data, solvers, and both physical and soft sensors. To facilitate data collection and storage, this knowledge base is often maintained in an on-premises database, as shown in Figure 1 b, ensuring secure and rapid access to process data for real-time monitoring. When the initial stage fails to capture all necessary QIVs for effective monitoring, the approach pivots to the 2 Innovations in Chemical Engineering www.sciencedirect.com Current Opinion in Chemical Engineering 2025, 48 :101150 second stage, which is agentified modeling, combining mechanistic process models with artificial intelligence. Here, we distinguish between traditional ’ AI agents ’ that perform specialized data processing and predictive tasks, and ’ Agentic AI ’ that imparts autonomous, decision- making capabilities to the system. The system leverages industrial communication protocols such as MQTT (Message Queuing Telemetry Transport), a lightweight messaging protocol for efficient data streaming and processing, and I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit), a serial communication protocol used for connecting sensors and actuators to the control system, as depicted in Figure 1 b. If sufficient process knowledge is available, the system leverages this to ‘close the loop’ with targeted generative models; if not, hybrid modeling techniques are em- ployed to develop generative agents (or soft sensors) that predict or measure the desired process parameters. The integrated network of agents feeds directly into the control system, enabling it to make informed, real-time decisions. Figure 1 Current Opinion in Chemical Engineering (a) The systematic approach for generative modeling, including 1) creating a process and instrumentation workflow, 2) agentified modeling for real- time monitoring, and 3) give agency to the control system. (b) Agent models and their connection to SCADA and control system. Industrial generative modeling in complex systems Boskabadi et al. 3 www.sciencedirect.com Current Opinion in Chemical Engineering 2025, 48 :101150 In the third stage, the accumulated data — whether directly measured or generated via predictive modeling — are seamlessly integrated into the control system, endowing it with the agency to make real-time deci- sions. This control system often includes components like SCADA for high-level process supervision and PLC (Programmable Logic Controller) for managing actuators and executing control commands, as illustrated in Figure 1 b. In this stage, the control system not only utilizes outputs from traditional AI agents (as established in stage 2) but is also empowered by Agentic AI to au- tonomously execute decision-making and adapt to changing process conditions in real time. This integra- tion transforms the control system into an adaptive, au- tonomous entity that continuously monitors process variables and adjusts operational parameters to maintain optimal performance. sections.heading: Case 1: A motivating example of generative
sections.text: modeling as a soft sensor in motor sports Motorsport is a high-stakes environment where split- second decisions can define the difference between victory and defeat. In such a setting, real-time analytics are not just beneficial — they are essential. Motorsports teams like Andretti Autosport rely on real-time data to make immediate adjustments during a race, from tire pressure and degradation monitoring to optimizing fuel consumption and adjusting race strategy based on evol- ving track conditions and weather. The literature on motorsports analytics has highlighted several key algorithmic and data-driven approaches aimed at improving performance and strategic decision- making during races. One major area of focus is optimal trajectory planning, where machine learning models are developed to determine the fastest possible racing lines, enabling real-time adjustments in response to changing track conditions [25] . Energy management strategies represent another significant domain of research, espe- cially for hybrid vehicles. Optimization algorithms in this area consider not only vehicle dynamics but also com- petitors’ behavior to minimize lap times while staying within energy constraints [26] . Predictive modeling is also a prominent focus, with data-driven approaches being used to identify key factors that influence race outcomes, such as yellow flag probability, vehicle dy- namics, tire performance, and environmental conditions. These models support more effective strategic planning and race execution [27] . These studies underscore the critical importance of real- time data processing and predictive analytics in motor- sports. The integration of advanced generative AI models extends this body of research by providing in- stantaneous, predictive insights that complement ex- isting analytical techniques. Specifically, generative models can create synthetic data that closely mirrors actual sensor measurements, enabling deeper insights into vehicle behavior and the wear of critical compo- nents. This approach addresses several gaps identified in the literature, pushing the application of data analytics in motorsports further into real-time, decision-support contexts. The generative AI solution developed by Zapata AI for Andretti Autosport [28] complements the existing lit- erature by integrating advanced predictive analytics and real-time synthetic data generation into an edge-to-cloud architecture tailored for high-performance environments like racing. This approach effectively addresses the cri- tical need for low-latency, high-reliability decision sup- port that traditional algorithmic methods in the literature often overlook. The system architecture ( Figure 2 ) is designed to handle the intense computational demands of motorsport ana- lytics through a combination of edge and cloud-based processing: • Transportable edge deployment . The core of the solution is a transportable edge computing unit equipped with high-performance GPUs(Graphics Processing Units). This hardware is deployed trackside, enabling the immediate ingestion and processing of telemetry data directly from the cars. By processing data at the edge, the system minimizes latency, providing real-time feedback on critical metrics like tire degradation, fuel 4 Innovations in Chemical Engineering www.sciencedirect.com Current Opinion in Chemical Engineering 2025, 48 :101150 efficiency, and component wear. This contrasts with cloud-only solutions in the literature, which often introduce delays due to data transmission. Internet connectivity at some tracks is often unpredictable in terms of reliability and latency. • Cloud-based model training and synchronization . The cloud infrastructure serves as a scalable environment for training generative models on large datasets, in- cluding historical telemetry and synthetic data gen- erated during prior races. sections.heading: Case 2: Plant-wide manufacturing process
sections.text: monitoring The production of sugar from sugar beets is a highly in- tricate and multistage process carried out within specia- lized sugar factories. This journey begins with trucks Figure 3 Current Opinion in Chemical Engineering Technical implementation Race Strategy services. Industrial generative modeling in complex systems Boskabadi et al. 7 www.sciencedirect.com Current Opinion in Chemical Engineering 2025, 48 :101150 delivering sugar beets to the factory, where they are in- itially assessed at the weighbridge. The process then pro- ceeds through several critical steps, including sampling, unloading, washing, slicing, and extraction in the extraction tower. The extracted juice is purified in a dedicated pur- ification unit before undergoing evaporation, crystal- lization, centrifugation, and drying. The resulting sugar is subsequently stored in silos until it is dispatched from the service center. Among all these stages, crystallization is particularly significant, as it has a profound impact on the final specifications of the sugar crystals, energy consump- tion, and the factory’s overall carbon footprint. When the crystal size distribution falls outside the desired range, the material must be recycled for remelting and recrystalliza- tion, adding complexity to the operation. The crystallization of sugar from sugar beet syrup is a complex and dynamic process involving the transformation of syrup into massecuite. This process is inherently non- linear and nonstationary, shaped by intricate mechanisms of nucleation, crystal growth, and aggregation [29] . Despite its critical importance, there is no comprehensive me- chanistic model available to accurately describe the inter- play between crystallization dynamics and operating conditions. As a result, current control strategies largely rely on the online monitoring of key process parameters. However, in industrial batch crystallizers, accurately mea- suring the crystal size distribution, a key QIV, remains a significant challenge [30] . This case study highlights collaborative research conducted by Nordzucker and the Technical University of Denmark, which aimed to address this challenge. The research uti- lized process knowledge and artificial intelligence to model the complex dynamics and nonlinearities in the original dataset. The focus was on generating the Brix index, a critical measure of dissolved solids in a liquid, as a key QIV representing crystal size distribution. The study adopted a hybrid approach, combining process control expertise with machine learning techniques. By leveraging easily measurable variables, such as temperature and pressure, the model successfully generated the Brix index for real-time process monitoring. This information supported decision-making and complemented batch-pro- cessing operations. Further information regarding perfor- mance and validation of the developed soft sensor for sugar crystallization has been reported by Boskabadi et al. [31] . The results demonstrated that the soft sensor devel- oped in this study effectively predicted the Brix index, capturing the process’s dynamic and nonlinear characteristics. This aligns with steps 2 and 3 of the systematic approach presented in Figure 1 , where generative modeling enables real-time monitoring and decision-making. By implementing this monitoring system and granting agency to the control system, batch residence time during crystallization was sig- nificantly reduced. Consequently, this leads to lower energy consumption and CO ₂ emissions while in- creasing production capacity. The objective of deploying a soft sensor in plant-wide manufacturing should be to enhance process monitoring reliability and ensure alignment with Industry 4.0 goals. sections.heading: Case 3: Predictive consumer product
sections.text: modeling The structure and chemical composition of hair fibers have been well-understood for many years. However, due to the vast diversity in hair types, the cosmetic in- dustry faces challenges in meeting the unique needs of each consumer [32] . This has led to a rapid shift toward product customization and the integration of digitally connected beauty tools [33,34] . In response to these trends, Henkel Consumer Brands introduced the Sal- onLab Ecosystem in 2018 ( Figure 4 ). This innovative approach is built upon three key elements: (a) advanced hair analysis, (b) understanding consumer needs and preferences, and (c) personalized product formulation. Step 1: Advanced hair analysis The process begins with a smart device equipped with a near-infrared (NIR) sensor and a visible light sensor to analyze the hair fiber. NIR spectroscopy is a well-es- tablished, highly effective analytical method for non- destructive examination of hair characteristics. Recent advancements in sensor technology and miniaturization have enabled the application of this technique outside traditional laboratory settings. This allows for precise identification of the hair cortex’s chemical composition and the effect of hair care products. Through NIR analysis, much information about the hair can be obtained, including two critical metrics: cysteic 8 Innovations in Chemical Engineering www.sciencedirect.com Current Opinion in Chemical Engineering 2025, 48 :101150 acid concentration (a degradation product of cystine) and the ‘bulk effect’ of care products on the hair. The re- sulting spectral data show excellent correlation with sensory assessments, enabling a rational and systematic classification of both the hair and hair-plus-product based on their current condition. To achieve a compre- hensive hair diagnosis, the actual color of the hair fiber is also measured using a visible light sensor. The quantification of cysteic acid, prediction of the ‘bulk effect,’ and detection of hair color are all achieved through the development of chemometric machine learning models. These models are trained on a diverse database containing hair samples from various origins, colors, and conditions, ensuring robust and accurate analysis. Step 2: Visual assessment and consumer consultation In the next phase, a visual evaluation is conducted to assess factors such as scalp condition, previous treat- ments, hair length, thickness, etc. In addition, user ex- pectations regarding desired outcomes (e.g. volume, shine, smoothness, strength) are gathered through a consultation application. This dual approach ensures a comprehensive understanding of the consumer’s specific needs and hair health. Step 3: Customized shampoo formulation All collected data — from both the scientific analysis and the consumer consultation — are integrated into a de- cision matrix. This matrix guides the creation of a cus- tomized shampoo formulation tailored to the individual’s unique hair profile and desired results. The SalonLab concept has been introduced in professional hair salons worldwide, providing personalized solutions for a diverse range of hair types. Expanding with generative AI Building on this success, Henkel Consumer Brands is now leveraging Generative AI algorithms to scale the concept further. By analyzing consumer preferences on a mass scale, inputs in textual format can be fed into customized LLMs. These models accurately interpret specific consumer desires and seamlessly integrate them with the formula generation system, enabling even more precise and personalized hair care solutions ( Figure 4 ). Employing Generative AI would not be limited to only understanding consumer sentiment, but it can also be used for innovation and discovery at the chemical and molecular level. sections.heading: Case 4: Biomanufacturing process scale-up
sections.text: with quantum and classical agents Bioprocess engineering requires information at various levels of granularity across scales like metabolic path- ways, reaction kinetics, reactor specifications, and inter- action of the micro to the macroscale and vice versa [35,36] . While many of these phenomena can be mod- eled mechanistically, engineering towards the goal of maximizing process throughput and other constraints satisfaction requires tools from artificial intelligence (AI) such as search, optimization, sampling, and machine learning to model process correlations [37,38•,39] . The complexity is further enhanced due to the unavailability of data from many critical microscale states such as metabolic fluxes, cell morphology, viability, and so on, not disregarding the stochasticity in the dynamics of the individual cells and observability limitations of the pro- cess. Developing systematic algorithms validated by experiments forms the foundation for developing pipe- lines for the accelerated scale-up of manufacturing bio- molecules. Some of the measurables that affect the growth of the cell are O 2 level, CO 2 level, nutrient concentration, pH, and temperature [40–42] . In the context of certain species, like microalgae, light irra- diance also plays a key role [43,44] . Currently, there is a lack of transferability of measure- ment technologies and scale-up strategies. It is also computationally intensive to estimate the state of a cell in a bioreactor given just the operating conditions of the bioreactor. Some aspects seen during experiments are to estimate the state of a bioreactor from macroscopic measurements and process causations obtained from controlled experiments . Another explored alternative is to use process information to trigger metabolic pathways to aid in manufacturing desirable compounds, avoiding byproducts and inhibitors. Advanced monitoring from imaging, spectroscopy, and capacitance probes has made it possible to have at-line/ on-line monitors. While great instrumentational ad- vancements, sporadic measurements, and transferability of results post-calibration are a hindrance. However, some online instrumentation and independent experiments aided by mechanistic knowledge can be leveraged to generate explainable monitoring solutions. Generative models are a class of machine learning algorithms de- signed to understand and replicate complex data dis- tributions. By leveraging these models, researchers and practitioners in biomanufacturing can unlock several critical capabilities: 1. De Novo Design: Generative models can create en- tirely new biological sequences, such as proteins or DNA/RNA sequences, tailored for specific functions or properties. For instance, designing enzymes with higher stability or therapeutic proteins with improved efficacy. 2. Optimization of Bioprocesses: These models enable the fine-tuning of fermentation conditions, media formulations, and process parameters to maximize yield and quality. 3. Predictive Insight: By learning from existing datasets, generative models can predict the outcomes of ge- netic modifications, aiding in the development of engineered organisms for bioproduction. 4. Personalization: In the context of personalized med- icine, generative models can assist in crafting patient- specific biologics, such as tailored vaccines or cell therapies. This example aims to create a transferable real-time data-agnostic monitoring system, with process knowl- edge gained from micro and macroscale experiments by integrating a diverse range of offline sensors that can help in generating fast scale-up solutions. With inclusion of hydrodynamics, it is important to look at variations in the reactor to account for different environments ex- perienced by the organism. sections.heading: Conclusions and perspectives
sections.text: Generative models have demonstrated significant poten- tial in addressing diverse industrial challenges. This study presents a systematic approach to generative modeling and agentic AI for process system engineering. This sys- tematic approach consists of three different steps, in- cluding creating the process and instrumentation process diagram for the desired process. Then, the measuring process variables are determined using direct measure- ment. In this step, if measuring the process variable is not directly possible, generative modeling considering both process knowledge and artificial intelligence plays a cru- cial role in monitoring variables. Finally, this information could be used for different purposes, including process control, optimization, and scale-up. To investigate this systematic approach, four case stu- dies showcasing the application of generative modeling in real-time motorsport optimization, customer-focused product design, the development of soft sensors for sustainable food manufacturing, and decision-making tools for biomanufacturing scale-up were investigated. These examples highlight the versatility of generative models in understanding and replicating complex data distributions, enabling their application in varied in- dustrial domains. While the promise of industrial Agentic AI and gen- erative modeling is vast, several key limitations must be addressed before they can be more widely adopted in chemical engineering. High-quality, representative da- tasets remain scarce or costly to obtain, constraining model training and generalization. Seamless integration with wet-lab experiments is often hindered by mis- matched data formats and timescales, complicating va- lidation and calibration efforts. The inherently ‘black- box’ nature of many generative architectures also raises concerns around interpretability and trust, especially in safety-critical applications. Moreover, real-time, agentic decision-making at scale demands significant computa- tional resources and robust edge-to-cloud infrastructure, which may not be available in all industrial settings. Finally, purely data-driven models can produce mis- leading or unsafe recommendations if not grounded in mechanistic process knowledge, highlighting the ne- cessity of hybrid approaches that blend domain expertise with agentic AI. By acknowledging these challenges alongside the de- monstrated benefits, we underscore the importance of ongoing research into explainable generative methods, self-adaptive calibration algorithms, and cost-effective data acquisition strategies. As these elements mature, the synergy between generative modeling and complex industrial systems will continue to drive innovation, ef- ficiency, and sustainability across chemical and biopro- cess engineering.
